Homarus gammarus , known as the European lobster or common lobster , is a species of clawed lobster from the eastern Atlantic Ocean , Mediterranean Sea and parts of the Black Sea . It is closely related to the American lobster , H. americanus . It may grow to a length of 60 cm ( 24 in ) and a mass of 6 kilograms ( 13 lb ) , and bears a conspicuous pair of claws . In life , the lobsters are blue , only becoming " lobster red " on cooking . Mating occurs in the summer , producing eggs which are carried by the females for up to a year before hatching into planktonic larvae . Homarus gammarus is a highly esteemed food , and is widely caught using lobster pots , mostly around the British Isles . 
 Homarus gammarus is a large crustacean , with a body length up to 60 centimetres ( 24 in ) and weighing up to 5 – 6 kilograms ( 11 – 13 lb ) , although the lobsters caught in lobster pots are usually 23 – 38 cm ( 9 – 15 in ) long and weigh 0 @.@ 7 – 2 @.@ 2 kg ( 1 @.@ 5 – 4 @.@ 9 lb ) . Like other crustaceans , lobsters have a hard exoskeleton which they must shed in order to grow , in a process called ecdysis ( moulting ) . This may occur several times a year for young lobsters , but decreases to once every 1 – 2 years for larger animals . 
 The first pair of pereiopods is armed with a large , asymmetrical pair of claws . The larger one is the " crusher " , and has rounded nodules used for crushing prey ; the other is the " cutter " , which has sharp inner edges , and is used for holding or tearing the prey . Usually , the left claw is the crusher , and the right is the cutter . 
 The exoskeleton is generally blue above , with spots that coalesce , and yellow below . The red colour associated with lobsters only appears after cooking . This occurs because , in life , the red pigment astaxanthin is bound to a protein complex , but the complex is broken up by the heat of cooking , releasing the red pigment . 
 The closest relative of H. gammarus is the American lobster , Homarus americanus . The two species are very similar , and can be crossed artificially , although hybrids are unlikely to occur in the wild since their ranges do not overlap .  Female H. gammarus reach sexual maturity when they have grown to a carapace length of 80 – 85 millimetres ( 3 @.@ 1 – 3 @.@ 3 in ) , whereas males mature at a slightly smaller size . Mating typically occurs in summer between a recently moulted female , whose shell is therefore soft , and a hard @-@ shelled male . The female carries the eggs for up to 12 months , depending on the temperature , attached to her pleopods . Females carrying eggs are said to be " berried " and can be found throughout the year . 
 The eggs hatch at night , and the larvae swim to the water surface where they drift with the ocean currents , preying on zooplankton . This stage involves three moults and lasts for 15 – 35 days . After the third moult , the juvenile takes on a form closer to the adult , and adopts a benthic lifestyle . The juveniles are rarely seen in the wild , and are poorly known , although they are known to be capable of digging extensive burrows . It is estimated that only 1 larva in every 20 @,@ 000 survives to the benthic phase . When they reach a carapace length of 15 mm ( 0 @.@ 59 in ) , the juveniles leave their burrows and start their adult lives .

It is also present in most of the Mediterranean Sea , only missing from the section east of Crete , and along only the north @-@ west coast of the Black Sea .  The species can be divided into four genetically distinct populations , one widespread population , and three which have diverged due to small effective population sizes , possibly due to adaptation to the local environment . The first of these is the population of lobsters from northern Norway , which have been referred to as the " midnight @-@ sun lobster " . The populations in the Mediterranean Sea are distinct from those in the Atlantic Ocean . The last distinct population is found in the Netherlands : samples from the <unk> were distinct from those collected in the North Sea or English Channel . 
 Attempts have been made to introduce H. gammarus to New Zealand , alongside other European species such as the edible crab , Cancer pagurus . Between 1904 and 1914 , one million lobster larvae were released from hatcheries in Dunedin , but the species did not become established there . 
 Adult H. gammarus live on the continental shelf at depths of 0 – 150 metres ( 0 – 492 ft ) , although not normally deeper than 50 m ( 160 ft ) . They prefer hard substrates , such as rocks or hard mud , and live in holes or crevices , emerging at night to feed .

 Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam , CB , CBE ( 15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976 ) was a senior commander in the Royal Australian Air Force ( RAAF ) . Born and educated in Tasmania , he joined the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934 . He specialised in flying instruction and navigation before the outbreak of World War II . In April 1941 , he became commanding officer of No. 2 Squadron , which operated Lockheed Hudsons . The squadron was deployed to Dutch Timor in December , and saw action against Japanese forces in the South West Pacific . After returning to Australia in February 1942 , Headlam held staff appointments and training commands , finishing the war a group captain . 
 Headlam served as Officer Commanding North @-@ Western Area in 1946 , and as Director of Training from 1947 to 1950 . In 1950 – 51 , during the Malayan Emergency , he was stationed at Singapore as commander of No. 90 ( Composite ) Wing and , later , RAF Tengah . He twice served as acting Air Member for Personnel , in 1957 and 1959 – 60 , receiving appointment as a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958 . Promoted air vice marshal , he successively held the positions of Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) Operational Command in 1961 – 62 , AOC No. 224 Group RAF from 1962 to 1965 during the Indonesia – Malaysia Konfrontasi , Deputy Chief of the Air Staff in 1965 – 66 , and AOC Support Command in 1966 – 67 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath in 1965 . Following a posting to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff from 1968 to 1971 , he retired from the Air Force and died in Melbourne five years later . 
 The son of farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam , Frank Headlam was born on 15 July 1914 in Launceston , Tasmania . He was schooled at <unk> College , Hobart , and matriculated in 1932 . He underwent flying instruction with No. 1 Flying Training School ( FTS ) at RAAF Point Cook , Victoria , and was commissioned as a pilot officer on 1 January 1935 .

No larger than a flight according to the official history of the pre @-@ war RAAF , Seaplane Squadron was part of No. 1 FTS and operated Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes , among other types . During this posting Headlam was promoted to flying officer , on 1 July 1935 , and wrote a paper on national defence in which he suggested that with " strong air forces , naval forces ( including submarines ) , and fixed defences , Australia may be made practically invulnerable " . According to Air Force historian Alan Stephens , this paper " in effect , defined the ' anti @-@ lodgment ' concept which has been a persistent feature of RAAF strategic thinking " . 
 Headlam completed a flying instructors course in July 1936 and joined the staff of No. 1 FTS . He was promoted to flight lieutenant on 1 March 1937 . Commencing in July 1938 , he was one of six students to take part in the RAAF 's first Long Specialist Navigation Course , run by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook . The course involved several epic training flights that attracted considerable media attention , including a twelve @-@ day , 10 @,@ 800 @-@ kilometre ( 6 @,@ 700 mi ) round @-@ Australia trip by three Avro Ansons , one of which was piloted by Headlam , in November . The following month , Headlam led the three Ansons on a six @-@ day journey back and forth over Central Australia . He subsequently passed the navigation course with a special distinction . On 27 January 1939 he was posted to RAAF Station Laverton , Victoria , as a flight commander . He served initially with No. 2 Squadron , before transferring to No. 1 Squadron on 29 August . Both units operated Ansons . 
 Following the outbreak of World War II , No. 1 Squadron was engaged in convoy escort and maritime reconnaissance duties off south @-@ eastern Australia . Headlam continued to serve with the squadron as a flight commander until 15 January 1940 , when he was assigned to Headquarters Laverton as the station navigation officer . On 27 March he was posted to the staff of RAAF Headquarters , Melbourne . He was promoted to squadron leader on 1 June 1940 . Two weeks later he married Katherine Bridge at St Paul 's Anglican Church in Frankston ; the couple would have a son and a daughter . 
 Headlam was given command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton on 15 April 1941 , and raised to wing commander on 1 July . Equipped with Lockheed Hudsons , the squadron mainly conducted maritime patrols in southern waters until 5 December , when four of its aircraft were ordered to Darwin , Northern Territory , in response to fears of Japanese aggression in the Pacific . On 7 December , this detachment established itself at Penfui , near Koepang in Dutch Timor , while No. 2 Squadron 's eight remaining Hudsons were stationed at Darwin on standby . The following day , aware that Australia was now at war in the Pacific , one of the Penfui @-@ based Hudsons attacked the Japanese <unk> Nanyo Maru , which was suspected of being a radio ship , and forced it aground . By 12 December , Headlam had transferred to Penfui as commanding officer of the base , as well as No. 2 Squadron .

Eastern Area Command , considered a de facto operational headquarters owing to the preponderance of combat units under its control , was reorganised as Home Command in October 1953 . He was promoted to acting air commodore in May . His appointment as aide @-@ de @-@ camp to Queen Elizabeth II was announced on 7 October 1954 . 
 Headlam was promoted to substantive air commodore on 1 January 1955 . In November he was posted to RAAF Overseas Headquarters , London , and the following year undertook studies at the Imperial Defence College . Returning to Australia , he served as acting Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air , Canberra , from 19 March to 21 October 1957 , between the terms of Air Vice Marshals Fred Scherger and Allan Walters , and again from 24 August 1959 to 28 March 1960 , between the terms of Walters and Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely . In this role Headlam occupied a seat on the Air Board , the service 's controlling body that comprised its senior officers and was chaired by the Chief of the Air Staff . He was also one of two RAAF representatives to serve on a committee , chaired by businessman William John Allison , examining conditions of defence service ; the committee 's recommendations led to a doubling of flight pay , among other improvements . Headlam 's other positions at the Department of Air included Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959 , and Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959 . The latter assignment put him in charge of the RAAF 's Directorate of Intelligence . Headlam was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire ( CBE ) in the 1958 Queen 's Birthday Honours , gazetted on 3 June . In May 1960 he became acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff . 
 On 30 January 1961 , Headlam joined the staff of Operational Command ( OPCOM ) , the successor organisation to Home Command , responsible for the direction of RAAF operational units . He took over as Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) OPCOM from Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock in April . Headlam was promoted to air vice marshal on 29 May . On 17 July 1962 , he was posted to RAAF Base Butterworth , Malaya , and took up the appointment of AOC No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore one week later . He was succeeded as AOC OPCOM by Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch . As AOC No. 224 Group , Headlam had overall responsibility for regional air defence and offensive air operations during the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962 , and the subsequent Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia that officially began the following month . Divorced from his first wife in 1956 , he married widowed social worker Vernon Spence at the Sydney registry office on 20 January 1964 . He handed over No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley @-@ Norris on 30 November . 
 Returning to Australia , Headlam became Deputy Chief of the Air Staff ( DCAS ) on 26 January 1965 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath ( CB ) " in recognition of distinguished service in the Borneo Territories " on 22 June . His tenure as DCAS coincided with the most significant rearmament program the Air Force had undertaken since World War II , and with manpower shortages stemming from this expansion and from Australia 's increasing involvement in the security of South East Asia . The first RAAF helicopters were committed to the Vietnam War towards the end of his term , and he travelled to Saigon with the Chief of the General Staff , Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton , in March 1966 to plan the deployment . The year before , Wilton had recommended to Air Marshal Murdoch , the Chief of the Air Staff , that two Iroquois be sent to Vietnam for familiarisation purposes ; Murdoch had rebuffed Wilton , and the RAAF helicopter squadron was considered underprepared for its army co @-@ operation role when it finally did deploy . On 1 January 1968 , Headlam was posted to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff . He served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from 17 November 1970 to 5 June 1971 . 
 Returning to Australia in June 1971 , Headlam took resettlement leave before retiring from the Air Force on 3 August . He made his home in Melbourne , where he died aged 62 on 23 December 1976 , after a lengthy battle with cancer . Survived by his children and his second wife , he was given a private funeral and cremated at Springvale Crematorium .

 The current M @-@ 82 dates back to 1926 . It ran from US 31 in Hart to the northern junction of US 131 and M @-@ 46 in Howard City . rewritten: The European lobster ( *Homarus gammarus*) inhabits the eastern Atlantic, Mediterranean, and parts of the Black Sea.  A close relative of the American lobster (*H. americanus*), it can reach 60 cm long and weigh 6 kg, distinguished by its large claws.  Live lobsters are blue, turning the familiar red only upon cooking.  Summer mating results in eggs brooded by females for up to a year before hatching into larval plankton.  Highly prized as food,  *H. gammarus* is extensively harvested, particularly around the British Isles, using lobster pots.

The European lobster, *Homarus gammarus*, is a sizable crustacean, reaching up to 60 centimeters (24 inches) in length and 5-6 kilograms (11-13 pounds) in weight.  However, commercially caught lobsters typically measure 23-38 centimeters (9-15 inches) and weigh 0.7-2.2 kilograms (1.5-4.9 pounds).  Characteristic of crustaceans, their rigid exoskeleton necessitates periodic shedding—ecdysis or molting—to accommodate growth.  Younger lobsters molt several times annually, while this frequency reduces to once every one to two years in larger individuals.

A large, asymmetrical claw pair equips the first pereiopods.  One claw, the "crusher," possesses rounded nodules for crushing prey. The other, the "cutter," features sharp inner edges for holding and tearing it. Typically, the left claw functions as the crusher, while the right serves as the cutter.

Its upper shell is typically blue, marked with merging spots, while its underside is yellow.  Lobsters' characteristic red hue is a post-cooking phenomenon.  This is because the red pigment, astaxanthin, is bound within a protein complex in the live animal; heat breaks down this complex, revealing the red color.

Homarus americanus, the American lobster, is the closest relative of *H. gammarus*.  These species are nearly identical and can be artificially hybridized, though natural hybrids are rare due to non-overlapping habitats.  Distinguishing features, however, allow for species identification.

Female *H. gammarus* achieve sexual maturity at a carapace length of 80–85 mm (3.1–3.3 in), while males mature slightly smaller.  Summer mating involves a recently molted, soft-shelled female and a hard-shelled male.  The female then carries eggs, attached to her pleopods, for up to a year, depending on water temperature.  These egg-carrying ("berried") females are present year-round.

Nocturnal hatching initiates a larval phase where the offspring surface, becoming part of the ocean's currents and feeding on zooplankton.  This period, encompassing three molts, spans 15–35 days.  Following the final molt, a juvenile form emerges, transitioning to a bottom-dwelling existence.  While rarely observed and poorly understood, these juveniles are known to create extensive burrows.  Survival to this benthic stage is estimated at a mere 1 in 20,000 larvae.  Upon reaching a 15mm carapace length, juveniles abandon their burrows, commencing their adult lives.

The European lobster, *Homarus gammarus*, inhabits the northeastern Atlantic, ranging from Norway to the Azores and Morocco, excluding the Baltic Sea.  Its distribution also encompasses most of the Mediterranean, except for areas east of Crete, and the northwestern Black Sea coast.  Northernmost populations reside within the Arctic Circle, in Norwegian fjords.

Four genetically separate lobster populations exist: a large, widespread group, and three smaller, isolated groups likely shaped by local adaptation and limited genetic mixing.  One isolated group, the "midnight-sun lobster," inhabits northern Norway.  Mediterranean and Atlantic Ocean lobsters are genetically different.  Finally, a unique population in the Netherlands, distinct from those in the North Sea and English Channel, has been identified.

Efforts to establish the European species *H. gammarus* in New Zealand, mirroring similar attempts with species like the edible crab (*Cancer pagurus*), proved unsuccessful.  Despite the release of a million *H. gammarus* larvae in Dunedin between 1904 and 1914, the species failed to thrive.

inhabiting the continental shelf, adult *H. gammarus* are typically found at depths ranging from 0 to 150 meters (0-492 feet), rarely exceeding 50 meters (160 feet).  Their habitat preference includes hard substrates like rocks and firm mud, where they shelter in burrows and crevices, becoming active nocturnally to forage.

The European lobster, *Homarus gammarus*, is vulnerable to an unidentified disease caused by an unknown bacterium.  While common in American lobsters, this disease has only been observed in captive *H. gammarus*, with the possibility of prior American lobster (*H. americanus*) presence in the tanks not being excluded.

The European lobster, *Homarus gammarus*, is a highly prized culinary delicacy, referenced even in 17th-century English folk songs.  Commanding premium prices, it's sold fresh, frozen, canned, or as powder.  Both claws and tail offer excellent white meat, with most of the cephalothorax edible, excluding the gastric mill and gut.  Its market value surpasses that of the American lobster (*H. americanus*) by up to threefold, reflecting its superior taste.

Lobster fishing primarily employs traps, though lines baited with octopus or cuttlefish can also lure them for net or hand capture.  European and North African H. gammarus landings totaled 4,386 tonnes in 2008; 79% (3,462 tonnes) originated from the British Isles (including the Channel Islands).  The minimum legal carapace length for harvested H. gammarus is 87 mm (3.4 inches).

The International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature's Direction 51 designated *H. gammarus* as the type species of the genus *Homarus* Weber, 1795.  This clarified prior ambiguity stemming from the species' multiple names (including *Astacus marinus* Fabricius, 1775, and *Homarus vulgaris* H. Milne-Edwards, 1837) and the previous oversight of Weber's genus description, which Mary Rathbun later rediscovered, invalidating earlier type species assignments for *Homarus* Milne-Edwards, 1837.

Holthuis designated a lectotype specimen of *Homarus gammarus* in 1974.  Originating near Marstrand, Sweden (approximately 48 kilometers northwest of Gothenburg, at 57°53′N 11°32′E), this specimen, along with associated material, is now missing.

Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) senior officer Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam, CB, CBE (July 15, 1914 – December 23, 1976), a Tasmanian native, entered the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934.  Pre-war, he focused on flight instruction and navigation.  He commanded No. 2 Squadron, flying Lockheed Hudsons, from April 1941.  The squadron deployed to Dutch Timor in December 1941, engaging Japanese forces in the Southwest Pacific.  Returning to Australia in February 1942, Headlam served in staff and training roles, concluding the war as a group captain.

From 1946, Headlam commanded the North-Western Area, followed by his directorship of training (1947-1950).  During the Malayan Emergency (1950-51), he led No. 90 (Composite) Wing and RAF Tengah in Singapore.  He twice acted as Air Member for Personnel (1957 and 1959-60), receiving a CBE in 1958.  His promotion to Air Vice Marshal led to commands as AOC Operational Command (1961-62), AOC No. 224 Group RAF during the Indonesia-Malaysia Konfrontasi (1962-65), Deputy Chief of the Air Staff (1965-66), and AOC Support Command (1966-67).  He was appointed a CB in 1965.  After heading the Australian Joint Services Staff in London (1968-71), he retired, passing away in Melbourne five years later.

Born in Launceston, Tasmania on July 15, 1914, Frank Headlam was the son of farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam.  He attended <unk> College in Hobart, graduating in 1932.  Despite his parents' objections, he enlisted in the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) as an air cadet on January 16, 1934.  He trained at No. 1 Flying Training School (FTS), RAAF Point Cook, Victoria, and received his commission as a pilot officer on January 1, 1935.

Following a conversion course, Headlam joined the Point Cook Seaplane Squadron, a unit described in official pre-war RAAF records as no bigger than a flight.  Part of No. 1 FTS, the squadron operated Supermarine Southampton flying boats, de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes, and other aircraft.  He was promoted to Flying Officer on July 1st, 1935, during this posting.  That same year, Headlam authored a paper on national defense, advocating for Australia's invulnerability through "strong air and naval forces (including submarines), and fixed defenses."  Air Force historian Alan Stephens notes this paper essentially formulated the "anti-lodgment" strategy, a cornerstone of subsequent RAAF strategic planning.

In July 1936, Headlam finished a flight instructor's course and joined No. 1 FTS.  He was promoted to Flight Lieutenant on March 1, 1937.  Starting in July 1938, he was among six students in the RAAF's inaugural Long Specialist Navigation Course at Point Cook, led by Flight Lieutenants Garing and Murdoch.  This included several publicized long-range training flights, notably a twelve-day, 10,800-kilometer (6,700-mile) circumnavigation of Australia in November, with Headlam piloting one of three Avro Ansons.  In December, he led a six-day return flight across Central Australia.  He excelled, receiving special distinction upon course completion.  On January 27, 1939, he became a flight commander at RAAF Station Laverton, Victoria, initially with No. 2 Squadron, transferring to No. 1 Squadron on August 29; both operated Ansons.

After World War II began, No. 1 Squadron performed convoy protection and maritime surveillance missions along Australia's southeastern coast.  Headlam remained a flight commander until his January 15, 1940 transfer to Laverton Headquarters as navigation officer.  He then moved to RAAF Headquarters in Melbourne on March 27th.  A promotion to squadron leader followed on June 1st, 1940.  He married Katherine Bridge at St. Paul's Anglican Church, Frankston, two weeks later; they later had a son and a daughter.

On April 15, 1941, Headlam assumed command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton, receiving a promotion to Wing Commander on July 1st.  Equipped with Lockheed Hudsons, the squadron primarily patrolled southern waters until December 5th, when four aircraft were deployed to Darwin due to escalating Japanese aggression.  These aircraft established a detachment at Penfui, near Koepang in Dutch Timor, on December 7th, while the remaining eight Hudsons remained on standby in Darwin.  The next day, following Australia's entry into the Pacific War, a Hudson from Penfui attacked and beached the Japanese Nanyo Maru, suspected of being a radio ship.  By December 12th, Headlam had relocated to Penfui, taking command of both the base and No. 2 Squadron.

In January 1942, No. 2 Squadron's planes were stationed across Penfui, an unspecified island, and Darwin.  From Penfui, they targeted Japanese vessels involved in the Celebes invasion. On January 11th, two Hudsons repelled an attack by three Japanese floatplanes, damaging or destroying them, while bombing a transport.  However, both Hudsons were lost the following day to Mitsubishi Zeros.  Penfui endured its first Japanese bombing raid on January 26th, with subsequent attacks damaging aircraft.  The surviving Hudsons relocated to Darwin, though Headlam and his team stayed to maintain Penfui's operational status for reconnaissance flights from Australia.  On February 18th, Headlam received orders to evacuate all but a small demolition team, assisted by Sparrow Force, to destroy the airfield. He returned to Darwin on the 19th, coinciding with the city's first Japanese air raid.  Four of No. 2 Squadron's Hudsons were destroyed; the rest were moved to Daly Waters, continuing reconnaissance and bombing missions over Timor.

Until May 12, 1942, Headlam served as Darwin's Headquarters North-Western Area Command's Controller of Operations.  He then commanded No. 2 Air Navigation School in Nhill, Victoria, utilizing Anson aircraft.  This school's personnel formed No. 97 (Reserve) Squadron in June.  Headlam subsequently led No. 2 Air Observer School (location unknown), also using Ansons, in Mount Gambier, South Australia, starting July 20, 1943.  Promoted to group captain on December 1, 1943, he became the first commanding officer of No. 3 [unit type unknown], operating Ansons and Fairey Battles from Port Pirie, on December 9.  Following this, he began studies at the RAAF Staff School in Mount Martha, Victoria, on October 2, 1944, before assuming the senior administrative staff officer role at North-Western Area Command on January 12, 1945.

In January 1946, Headlam assumed command of the North-Western Area.  Transferring to Britain later that year, he attended the RAF Staff College, Andover, and served at RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London.  Returning to Australia in November 1947, he became Director of Training at RAAF Headquarters.  He took command of No. 90 (Composite) Wing from Group Captain Heffernan in November 1950. Based at RAF Changi, Singapore, No. 90 Wing oversaw RAAF units—No. 1 (Bomber) Squadron (Avro Lincolns) and No. 38 (Transport) Squadron (Douglas C-47s)—operating during the Malayan Emergency.  Lincolns conducted area bombing and precision strikes, while Dakotas performed courier flights, VIP transport, medical evacuations, and troop/supply airlifts throughout Southeast Asia, including propaganda leaflet drops in Malaya.  On December 20th, Headlam was slightly injured when a No. 38 Squadron Dakota he co-piloted crash-landed after engine failure.  He became commander of RAF Tengah, Singapore, in August 1951, in addition to his No. 90 Wing command, relinquishing the latter in December 1951.

February 19, 1952, saw Headlam appointed Senior Air Staff Officer (SASO) at Eastern Area Command in Penrith, New South Wales.  His tenure coincided with the RAAF's rearmament, adopting English Electric Canberra bombers and CAC Sabre fighters.  This period also witnessed a significant restructuring of the Air Force, shifting from a geographical command structure to a functional one, creating Home (operational), Training, and Maintenance Commands.  Consequently, Eastern Area Command, effectively the operational headquarters, was reorganized as Home Command in October 1953.  Recognizing his "exceptional ability and devotion to duty," Headlam received the Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the 1954 New Year Honours, and was promoted to acting air commodore in May.  His appointment as aide-de-camp to Queen Elizabeth II followed on October 7, 1954.

On January 1, 1955, Headlam attained the rank of Air Commodore.  He then served at RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London (November 1955), followed by Imperial Defence College studies in 1956.  Back in Australia, he twice served as acting Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air, Canberra: March 19 to October 21, 1957 (between Scherger and Walters), and August 24, 1959 to March 28, 1960 (between Walters and Hely).  This role included a seat on the Air Board, the RAAF's governing body.  He also co-represented the RAAF on an Allison-chaired committee reviewing defense service conditions, resulting in doubled flight pay and other improvements.  Further roles at the Department of Air included Air Commodore Plans (October 1957-January 1959) and Director General Plans and Policy (January-August 1959), the latter overseeing the RAAF's intelligence directorate.  He received a CBE in the 1958 Queen's Birthday Honours (gazetted June 3rd) and became acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff in May 1960.

Assuming command of Operational Command (OPCOM), the RAAF's operational unit directorate, on January 30, 1961, Air Commodore Headlam succeeded Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock as Air Officer Commanding (AOC) in April.  He was promoted to air vice marshal on May 29.  A July 17, 1962 posting sent him to RAAF Butterworth, Malaya, where he became AOC No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore the following week.  Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch replaced him at OPCOM.  As AOC No. 224 Group, Headlam oversaw regional air defense and offensive operations during the December 1962 Brunei Rebellion and the subsequent Indonesian-Malaysian Konfrontasi.  Having divorced in 1956, he married social worker Vernon Spence in Sydney on January 20, 1964.  He relinquished command of No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley-Norris on November 30.

Upon his return to Australia, Headlam assumed the post of Deputy Chief of the Air Staff (DCAS) on January 26, 1965.  He received the Companion of the Order of the Bath (CB) on June 22nd, for distinguished service in Borneo.  His DCAS role overlapped with the RAAF's largest rearmament since WWII,  exacerbated by manpower shortages due to expansion and Australia's growing Southeast Asian commitments.  Toward the end of his tenure, the first RAAF helicopters deployed to Vietnam; he and Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton, Chief of the General Staff, visited Saigon in March 1966 to coordinate this.  The previous year, Wilton's proposal to send two Iroquois helicopters to Vietnam for familiarization, was rejected by Air Marshal Murdoch, the Chief of the Air Staff, leaving the RAAF helicopter squadron arguably underprepared for its army cooperation role. Headlam then succeeded Air Vice Marshal Douglas Candy as Air Officer Commanding Support Command, Melbourne, on August 8, 1966, a command formed in 1959 by merging Training and Maintenance Commands.  He was appointed Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff in London on January 1, 1968, and later served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from November 17, 1970 to June 5, 1971.

Headlam returned to Australia in June 1971, taking resettlement leave prior to his Air Force retirement on August 3rd.  He settled in Melbourne, where he passed away on December 23rd, 1976, at age 62, following a prolonged fight against cancer.  A private cremation service was held at Springvale Crematorium; he is survived by his children and his second wife.

Michigan's M-82, a state highway in the Lower Peninsula, connects Fremont and Howard City.  Running between Newaygo and Howard City, it passes through Fremont and skirts the Manistee National Forest's southern boundary.  This current alignment is the second M-82 in Michigan; the first, in the Upper Peninsula, existed by 1919. The Lower Peninsula route dates to the 1920s, although its termini have varied over time, extending as far west as New Era or Hesperia at different points.  Its present configuration was established in the late 1970s.

Starting at a tri-county junction with M-120 and B-96 west of Fremont, M-82 heads east.  M-120 forms the Newaygo-Oceana and Newaygo-Muskegon county lines, while B-96 marks the Oceana-Muskegon line.  Eastbound, M-82 follows 48th Street through farmland, becoming Main Street in Fremont's downtown before turning south onto Stewart Avenue.  Continuing east on 72nd Street, it passes through more farmland, transitioning to a more wooded area near the Muskegon River as it nears Newaygo.  M-82 then follows Fremont Street east to its concurrency with M-37, crossing the river together on State Street through downtown.  Separating south of downtown, M-82 continues east on 82nd Street, skirting the Manistee National Forest, finally terminating at US-131/M-46 (Exit 118) west of Howard City.

Michigan's Department of Transportation (MDOT) monitors roadway traffic as part of its maintenance duties, using average annual daily traffic (AADT) to measure volume.  In 2009, MDOT data showed M-82 west of Fremont had the highway's highest daily traffic at 16,532 vehicles. Conversely, the lowest volume, 4,018 vehicles, was recorded east of Newaygo.  Furthermore, no portion of this highway is designated as part of the National Highway System, a network crucial for national economic, defense, and transportation needs.

Established in 1926, the original M-82 ran from US 31 in Hart north to the US 131/M-46 junction in Howard City, traversing Ferry, Hesperia, and Fremont, and superseding M-41.  A 1936 M-46 extension between Newaygo and Howard City created a brief concurrency with M-82, resolving a routing gap in M-46.  This overlap was eliminated by 1938, truncating M-82 to its northern terminus at the M-37 intersection in Newaygo.  A realignment west of Ferry in late 1947 or early 1948 shifted the route westward to Shelby, abandoning its previous northwesterly course to Hart.

The western terminus of M-82 was shifted twice, in 1963 and 1964, bypassing Ferry and running from Hesperia to New Era.  Significant highway renumbering in Oceana County around 1969 affected M-82.  West of Hesperia, M-20 replaced M-82, terminating at New Era rather than Muskegon; south of Hesperia, M-120 replaced M-20.  M-82 was then shortened to run only between Hesperia and Newaygo.  Extension of M-82 eastward to Howard City occurred in 1973.  M-46's rerouting along US-131 south of Howard City to Cedar Springs, replacing M-57 between Cedar Springs and Casnovia, allowed M-82's reinstatement between Newaygo and Howard City.  Finally, in 1978, the M-82/M-120 concurrency ended, leaving M-82 truncated to its present western junction near Fremont.

Masashi Kishimoto's *Naruto* series features Shikamaru Nara (奈良シカマル, Nara Shikamaru) as a Konohagakure ninja.  A member of Team 10, alongside Ino Yamanaka and Choji Akimichi, under Asuma Sarutobi's leadership, Shikamaru is known for his intelligence, though often masked by a laid-back demeanor—a trait Kishimoto appreciates.  Beyond the manga and anime, Shikamaru appears in four *Naruto* films and various related media, such as video games and OVAs.

Shikamaru's character has garnered significant attention in numerous anime and manga reviews, frequently highlighting his blend of intelligence and laziness, and his impressive growth into a capable leader.  His evolution into an "unlikely hero" within the Naruto narrative was specifically praised by Anime News Network.  This popularity extends to the fanbase, reflected in consistently high rankings in popularity polls and the release of various Shikamaru-themed merchandise, such as action figures, keychains, and patches.

Kishimoto admires Shikamaru's laid-back genius, a stark contrast to Sasuke's sharp intellect and abrasive demeanor.  He even jokingly professed a desire to marry Shikamaru (were he female), highlighting Shikamaru's predicted life success.  Designing Shikamaru's Part II look, Kishimoto aimed for distinctiveness, even while using a common vest.  He cleverly placed the forehead protector on his arm to showcase his hairstyle.

Shikamaru's debut is during the Chunin Exams, annual tests for ninjas seeking promotion.  He's on Team 10 with Choji Akimichi and Ino Yamanaka.  Known for his apathy and aversion to exertion, Shikamaru possesses exceptional intelligence; his teacher, Asuma Sarutobi, assessed his IQ above 200.  His skills center on the Shadow Imitation Technique (Kagemane no Jutsu), a clan-specific ability letting him merge shadows, immobilizing opponents and forcing them to copy his actions.  His shadow manipulation evolves throughout the series.  By Part II, he expertly uses multiple shadow-based techniques simultaneously, even lifting his shadow to interact with objects, impaling enemies with shadow tendrils or employing them to hurl weapons.

Showing little enthusiasm, Shikamaru faced the Chunin Exams.  He bested Temari of Sunagakure, but conceded the fight due to depleted chakra.  Nevertheless, his strategic brilliance against her impressed the examiners, resulting in his unique promotion to Chunin amongst his cohort.  His new rank brought the responsibility of leading a team to stop Sasuke Uchiha's defection to Otogakure.  While Shikamaru's team overcame Otogakure's opposition, Sasuke ultimately evaded capture.

Part II sees Shikamaru tasked with finding two Akatsuki members.  His team locates them, but despite his efforts, the immortal Akatsuki member <unk> kills Asuma Sarutobi.  Following Asuma's funeral, Shikamaru, with Team 10 and Kakashi Hatake, seeks revenge. While others confront <unk>'s partner <unk>, Shikamaru avenges Asuma by defeating <unk> and ensuring the body's disappearance.  He then pledges to protect Kurenai <unk> and Asuma's child.  Later, he joins the Fourth Division with Temari and <unk>, serving as Gaara's proxy general.  The epilogue reveals Shikamaru, after marrying Temari and fathering a son, <unk> Nara, fulfilling his ambition to advise the Seventh Hokage, Naruto.

Shikamaru appears in seven Naruto films:  He assists Naruto and Sakura against Haido in the second, battles stone soldiers briefly in the fourth, searches for the Land of Sky's base with Kakashi and Sai in the fifth, fights Hiruko's chimera in the sixth, combats the demon Satori in the eighth, and is a significantly different character in the ninth's Limited Tsukuyomi. In the tenth, he leads a team rescuing Hanabi Hyuga from Kinshiki Otsutsuki.  He's also in a third OVA tournament.  Shikamaru is a playable character in most Naruto video games, including the *Clash of Ninja* and *Ultimate Ninja* series, sometimes using Shadow Imitation Technique variations unseen in the anime or manga.  *Naruto Shippūden: Gekitō Ninja Taisen! EX 2* features his Part II design for the first time in a game.

Takashi Yano's *Shikamaru Hiden: A Cloud Drifting in Silent Darkness*, illustrated by Kishimoto, features Shikamaru as protagonist and narrator.  Two years post-Fourth Ninja War, Shikamaru, tasked with organizing the Shinobi Union, pursues a rogue ninja controlling the isolated Land of Silence, who aims to create a people's republic.  The story also follows Shikamaru's evolving relationship with Temari, concluding with his humorous struggles to name their newborn child years later.

Naruto's Shikamaru consistently ranked among the top ten characters in Weekly Shōnen Jump popularity polls, even achieving fourth place once.  A 2011 poll placed him ninth, surpassing Hinata but trailing Sasori.  His popularity extends to merchandise, encompassing action figures, keychains, and patches depicting both his earlier and later appearances.  Furthermore, NTT subscribers chose him as their sixteenth favorite black-haired male anime character, and CyberConnect2 CEO Hiroshi Matsuyama cited him as a personal favorite from the Naruto series.

Shikamaru's character has garnered significant attention from various media outlets covering manga, anime, and video games.  IGN highlighted him as a favorite, dubbing him the quintessential Gen X representative due to his apathy and untapped potential.  They lauded his leadership in episode 110, praising his ability to overcome laziness and effectively lead a Sasuke retrieval team, deeming his Chunin promotion justified.  Anime News Network echoed this, citing his unlikely heroism as a series highlight.  Following the mission's failure in episode 135, IGN celebrated Shikamaru's emotional response to his friends' injuries, predicting his growth into a stronger leader.  Mania Entertainment's Justin Rich praised his intelligence, calling him a captivating and exceptionally brilliant fighter within the shonen anime genre.  Fellow Mania reviewer Dani Moure singled out his Chunin Exams battle with Temari as a standout among supporting character fights.

Meridian, Mississippi's sixth-largest city, serves as Lauderdale County's seat and anchors the Meridian Micropolitan Statistical Area.  Its strategic location along major highways places it 93 miles (150 km) east of Jackson, 154 miles (248 km) west of Birmingham, Alabama, 202 miles (325 km) northeast of New Orleans, and 231 miles (372 km) southeast of Memphis.

Founded in 1860 where the Mobile and Ohio Railroad and the Southern Railway of Mississippi converged, Meridian's prosperity stemmed from its rail connections and the commerce they facilitated, establishing it as a vital trading hub.  However, the city suffered greatly during the Civil War when General William Tecumseh Sherman's forces razed much of it during the February 1864 Battle of Meridian.

Post-war reconstruction ushered in a "Golden Age" for the city, which became Mississippi's largest between 1890 and 1930, a major Southern manufacturing hub with 44 daily train arrivals and departures.  Its 1906 Union Station now serves as a multimodal transportation center, connecting to Meridian Transit, Greyhound, and Trailways buses, averaging 242,360 annual passengers. While the railroad's decline slowed economic growth, diversification into healthcare, military, and manufacturing sectors created the largest employment areas by 2010.  The 2008 census showed 38,232 city residents, but a broader metropolitan area—232,900 within a 45-mile (72 km) radius and 526,500 within 65 miles (105 km)—boasts a workforce of 104,600 and 234,200 respectively, significantly contributing to the city's economy.

Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field, employing over 4,000 people, are the area's primary military installations.  NAS Meridian houses the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy and Mississippi's first Department of Homeland Security office.  Key Field, named for the Key brothers' 1935 endurance flight record, hosts the 186th Air Refueling Wing (Air National Guard) and supports the 185th Aviation Brigade (Army National Guard).  Locally, Rush Foundation Hospital is the largest non-military employer, with a workforce of 2,610.

Meridian boasts a rich cultural landscape, including the Riley Center, Meridian Museum of Art, Meridian Little Theatre, and Meridian Symphony Orchestra.  The city's history is also reflected in its two former Carnegie libraries—one each for white and African American residents.  The now-demolished Carnegie Branch Library exemplified the segregated system of library provision common in the Southern US during that era.

Meridian, the future site of the Mississippi Arts and Entertainment Center, boasts a rich history.  It's the birthplace of Jimmie Rodgers, the "Father of Country Music," whose life and career are commemorated at Highland Park's museum, alongside steam-engine era railroad artifacts.  The park also features the world's only two-row stationary Dentzel menagerie carousel, a National Historic Landmark.  Other notable Meridian residents include Miss America 1986, Susan Akin; civil rights activist James Chaney, murdered in 1964; and Hartley Peavey, founder of Peavey Electronics.  The city's federal courthouse hosted the 1966-67 trial of those involved in Chaney's murder, marking a landmark moment: the first conviction of a white official for a civil rights killing by a white jury.

The land encompassing present-day Meridian was originally home to the Choctaw Nation.  The Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek (1830), a consequence of the Indian Removal Act, ceded this territory to the United States.  Following treaty ratification,  European-American colonists started settling the area.

Meridian's first settler, Richard McLemore, spurred growth by offering free land from his 2,000-acre federal grant.  However, most of this land was purchased in 1853 by Alabama lawyer Lewis A. Ragsdale.  John T. Ball, a Kemper County merchant, acquired the remaining 80 acres.  Ragsdale and Ball, now considered Meridian's founders, subsequently began plotting building lots on their respective properties.

A naming dispute arose for the new settlement.  Ball and the city's industrialists favored "Meridian," viewing it as equivalent to "junction."  Agrarian residents, however, preferred "<unk>", a Native American term for "mad river," after a local creek.  Ragsdale suggested "Ragsdale City."  Ball's Mobile and Ohio Railroad station sign alternated daily between "Meridian" and "<unk>".  Ultimately,  the railroad's expansion and influx of workers decided the issue, permanently settling on "Meridian."  The town officially became Meridian on February 10, 1860.

In 1861, Meridian was a small village whose strategic railroad location prompted the Confederacy to build several military installations.  The 1864 Battle of Meridian saw General Sherman's Union forces raze much of the town, including its railroad lines, arsenal, and supply depots.  Sherman famously declared Meridian's complete destruction, encompassing its "depots, storehouses, arsenal, hospitals, offices, hotels, and cantonments."  Remarkably, the railroads were fully operational again within 26 days.  However, racial tensions persisted through Reconstruction, culminating in a significant riot in 1871 following a destructive fire.

Meridian flourished after the Civil War, enjoying a "Golden Age" from 1880 to 1910 fueled by railroad expansion and subsequent industrial growth.  This led to a population surge and a thriving downtown commercial sector.  From 1890 to 1930, Meridian was Mississippi's largest city and a major Southern manufacturing hub.  This period saw the construction of many of its landmark buildings, such as the Grand Opera House (1890), Wechsler School (1894), two Carnegie libraries (1913), and the city's tallest skyscraper, the <unk> Building (1929).

Meridian's growth continued, fueled by a commission government that attracted 90 new factories in 1913 and a thriving auto industry throughout the 1920s.  Despite the 1929 stock market crash and the subsequent Great Depression, new businesses continued to locate there. Reflecting the era's escapism, the S. H. Kress & Co. store, designed to offer affordable luxury, and the Temple Theater opened downtown.  The federal courthouse, a WPA project, was completed in 1933.

Following a short economic downturn post-Depression, America's entry into World War II revitalized the railroad industry.  Crucial for moving fuel and materials for military production, Meridian re-established itself as a regional rail hub. This economic resurgence lasted until the 1950s, when automobiles and the Interstate Highway System eclipsed rail passenger traffic.  The subsequent railroad decline led to substantial job losses and a population decrease as workers sought opportunities elsewhere.

Meridian, Mississippi, served as a hub for Civil Rights activism during the 1960s, housing a Council of Federated Organizations (COFO) office and numerous other activist groups.  Local residents, including James Chaney, collaborated with northern volunteers like Michael Schwerner, his wife Rita, and Andrew Goodman, to establish a community center and voter registration drive for African Americans.  This activism fueled racial tensions and violence from local whites.  In June 1964, Chaney, Schwerner, and Goodman traveled to Neshoba County to support a firebombed Black church, disappearing that night on their return journey.  A subsequent extensive FBI investigation uncovered their murdered bodies, buried in an earthen dam, two months later.

A federal Meridian court found seven Klansmen, one a deputy sheriff, guilty of violating victims' civil rights in the murders of civil rights workers; three were acquitted.  This marked the first conviction of a white official for a civil rights killing by a white jury.  The state reopened the case in 2005, leading to Edgar Ray Killen's manslaughter conviction and a 60-year prison sentence.  Meridian subsequently commemorated victim James Chaney by renaming a street and establishing an annual memorial.

Post-1960s highway construction facilitated suburban expansion, drawing residents from the city center to northern housing developments.  Subsequently, as commercial activity shifted away from the downtown area, the city responded by establishing several historic districts during the 1970s and 80s to safeguard its architectural heritage.  This effort culminated in the 1979 creation of the Meridian Historic Districts and Landmarks Commission and the launch of the Meridian Main Street program in 1985.

Meridian Main Street spearheaded downtown revitalization efforts, starting with a 1997 Amtrak station modeled after the city's demolished Golden Age depot.  Further projects encompassed the 2001 Rosenbaum Building and 2002 Weidmann's Restaurant renovations, and advocacy for cohesive urban planning.  Partnering with The Riley Foundation, Meridian Main Street also oversaw the 2006 restoration and repurposing of the historic Grand Opera House as the Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and the Performing Arts.

The Alliance for Downtown Meridian assumed ownership of Meridian Main Street in late 2007, subsequently partnering with the Meridian Downtown Association to revitalize the downtown area.  This collaborative effort utilized the Alliance's resources—staff and facilities—to support both organizations, acting as a central point of contact.  While initial plans for the <unk> Building's renovation were underway, Mayor Cheri Barry's election in early 2010 led to their cancellation.  Currently, the Alliance fosters further development and restoration, focusing on businesses like restaurants, shops, and bars to enhance daytime and nighttime activity.  Meanwhile, the Meridian Downtown Association concentrates on boosting foot traffic through events, and the Meridian Main Street program provides support to existing downtown businesses.

Meridian's status as a railroad hub fueled the growth of its hotel industry.  Several large hotels, such as the Great Southern and Grand Avenue hotels, predate the city's "Golden Age," appearing before 1900.  The expansion of rail lines and the 1906 construction of the original Union Station spurred further hotel development to accommodate passengers and railway employees.  Notable examples include the Elmira (1905), Terminal (1910), Hotel Meridian (1907), and Union (1908) hotels.  The Union Hotel achieved a National Register of Historic Places listing in 1979, while Hotel Meridian and the Grand Avenue Hotel are recognized as contributing structures within the Meridian Urban Center Historic District.

The Lamar Hotel, an eleven-story testament to the city's booming economy, was constructed in 1927.  Recognized for its historical significance, it was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1979 and repurposed as a county annex.  Further acknowledging its importance, the hotel received Mississippi Landmark status in 1988.

Constructed in 1931, the E.F. Young Hotel was a cornerstone of the African-American business district that flourished west of the city center.  During the Jim Crow era, it served as a vital refuge, providing lodging to Black travelers in a city otherwise largely inaccessible to them.

Suburban growth during the 1960s and 70s led to the relocation of most hotels away from the city center.  However, the 2006 Riley Center renovation spurred renewed interest and a demand for a new downtown hotel.  The <unk> Building was suggested as a redevelopment site, but administrative changes hampered restoration efforts. To advocate for the building's revitalization, the <unk> Preservation Society launched in 2013, organizing first-floor tours and commemorative events to build public support.

Nine of Meridian's districts are on the National Register of Historic Places.  These include the Meridian Downtown Historic District, a consolidation of the Meridian Urban Center and Union Station Historic Districts.  The districts showcase a variety of architectural styles prevalent from the late 1800s and early 1900s, such as Queen Anne, Colonial Revival, Italianate, Art Deco, Late Victorian, and Bungalow.
