Since 1985, Meridian has utilized a "strong mayor" system, where the mayor, elected citywide every four years, serves as chief executive.  Five council members, each representing one of the city's five wards in single-member districts, are also elected every four years.  The mayor manages daily city operations, while the council, the legislative branch, establishes policy and approves the annual budget.

Located at 601 23rd Avenue, the City Hall, a National Register of Historic Places site, is led by Mayor Percy Bland.  Its city council comprises Dr. George M. Thomas (Ward 1), Kenneth Dustin Markham (Ward 2), Barbara Henson (Ward 3), Kim Houston (Ward 4), and Randy Hammon (Ward 5). Pam McInnis serves as council clerk.  The city's total workforce numbers 570 employees.

Following Hurricane Katrina in 2005, the city created its own Department of Homeland Security (DHS), a unique entity within the state.  This DHS, covering nine counties, received $2.5 million in grants (Mississippi Emergency Management Agency and others) to train regional law enforcement (passenger rail rescue) and offer public courses in basic handgun safety, first aid (Boy Scout certified), hunting, and firearms.  The department proved invaluable during crises, such as Hurricane Ivan (September 2005), providing shelter for 700 evacuees.  The city now heads a Mississippi DHS task force, uniting three nine-county teams.

The Meridian Police Department, led by Chief Lee <unk> since 2009, comprises 115 full-time officers, supplemented by part-time and reserve personnel.  Their Criminal Investigations Division handled 4000 cases in 2009, including 2000 felonies.  Reported crimes in 2009 totaled <unk>, a slight increase over the 2008 figure. Meridian claims the title of "safest city in Mississippi with a population exceeding 30,000."  Nearby in Lauderdale County sits the East Mississippi Correctional Facility, a GEO Group-operated prison under contract with the Mississippi Department of Corrections.  Meridian's Fire Department, headed by Chief Anthony Clayton, responded to over 1600 calls in 2009, encompassing 123 structural fires and 609 emergency medical calls.

Mississippi's Senate map carves the city into three districts.  The northernmost area is in the 31st District, represented by Terry Clark Burton (R).  A diagonal swath, from southwest to northeast, forms part of the 32nd District, held by Sampson Jackson II (D).  The remaining western and southeastern sections belong to the 33rd District, represented by <unk> Carmichael (R).  The House districts further subdivide the city into four.  House District 81 (Steven A. Horne, R) covers the south and east.  House District 82 encompasses the city's core, represented by Wilbert L. Jones (D), and is surrounded by House District 83 (Greg Snowden, R).  Finally, House District 84 (Tad Campbell, R) includes the western city area and a small northern portion.

Meridian, Mississippi, falls within the state's 3rd congressional district, currently represented by Republican Gregg Harper since 2009.  Lauderdale County, encompassing Meridian, has consistently voted Republican in every presidential election since 1972.  Before this Republican dominance, the county's white voters traditionally supported the Democratic Party, reflecting the state's long history as a one-party Democratic stronghold from the late 19th century onward.

Driven by complex social and economic forces, the city's population fluctuated since its inception.  Census data reveals consistent growth until 1970, with annual rates ranging from 0.2% to 165%.  A population decrease followed in 1970, with a slight rebound by 1980, before a gradual decline until the 21st century.  Between 1980 and 2000, a 14%+ decrease occurred.  The 2000 census recorded 39,968 residents, yielding a population density of 885.9 per square mile (342.0/km²).  By 2008, it ranked as the state's sixth-largest city, and further population growth was observed by 2010.

Meridian, the main city in the Meridian metropolitan area (encompassing Clarke, Kemper, and Lauderdale counties as of 2009), had a population of 106,139.  Within a 45-mile (72 km) radius, the population reached 232,900, expanding to 526,500 within a 65-mile (105 km) radius.

Despite fluctuating citywide population trends, the number and proportion of non-white residents have consistently increased.  The only exception was a decrease between 1960 and 1970, coinciding with a significant overall population drop.  The 2010 Census revealed a city population comprised of 61.55% African American, 35.71% White, 0.9% Asian, 0.2% Native American, <0.02% Pacific Islander, 0.59% from other races, and 0.89% from two or more races.  Hispanics or Latinos of any race constituted 1.75% of the total population.

In 2000, within Meridian city limits, 15,966 of the 17,890 housing units were occupied; 10,033 of these were occupied by families.  Occupied households included 31.1% with children under 18, 36.2% comprised of married couples, 23.3% headed by a female householder with no husband present, and 37.2% classified as non-family households.  Individual households constituted 33.2% of the total, with 14.0% occupied by a single person aged 65 or older. Average household and family sizes were 2.39 and 3.06 respectively, down from a 3.04 average household size in 1970.  Concurrently, Meridian's median age rose from 30.4 in 1970 to 34.6 in 2000.

Household median income in the city reached $25,085, while families earned a median of $31,062.  Median earnings were $29,404 for males and $19,702 for females.  City per capita income was $15,255.  Poverty affected 24.6% of families and 28.6% of the overall population;  this included 40.8% of children under 18 and 22% of residents aged 65 and older.

Meridian and its neighboring areas show high religious affiliation, with 65.2% of Lauderdale County residents identifying with a religious congregation, exceeding the national average of 50.2%.  In 2000, of those affiliated, the Southern Baptist Convention comprised 30,068 (59.0%), the United Methodist Church 9,469 (18.6%), and the Catholic Church 1,872 (3.7%).

German and Eastern European Jewish immigrants significantly contributed to Meridian's commercial growth, establishing numerous businesses and services.  The city's "Golden Age" was preceded by the founding of Congregation Beth Israel in 1868.  At its peak in 1927, Meridian boasted the state's largest Jewish population, numbering 575.  This community has since dwindled, with fewer than 40, primarily elderly, residents remaining today.

Meridian, situated in Lauderdale County within Mississippi's North Central Hills, covers 45.9 square miles (119 km²),  with 45.1 square miles (117 km²) being land and 0.8 square miles (2.1 km²) water, according to the U.S. Census Bureau.  Its location along major highways places it 93 miles (150 km) east of Jackson, Mississippi; 154 miles (248 km) west of Birmingham, Alabama; 202 miles (325 km) northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana; 231 miles (372 km) southeast of Memphis, Tennessee; and 297 miles (478 km) west of Atlanta, Georgia.  The surrounding landscape features cotton and corn fields, oak and pine forests, and a topography of clay hills and the bottomlands of the <unk> River's headwaters.

The city's center shows a graded, altered landscape, though the surrounding areas retain a gently rolling topography.  Scattered throughout are numerous small streams, with lakes and woodlands in the north and south.  <unk> Creek traverses the south, splitting into Gallagher's Creek, which flows through the city's heart.  Loper's Creek runs through the far west, while smaller tributaries, such as Shearer's Branch, Magnolia Creek, and Robbins Creek, are distributed across the city.

Meridian enjoys a humid subtropical climate.  Summer highs (June-August) average near 90°F (32°C), with lows around 70°F (21°C).  Winter temperatures (December-February) peak near 60°F (16°C) and dip to an average low of 35°F (2°C). July is the warmest month, averaging a high of 92.9°F (33.8°C), while January is the coldest, with average lows of 34.7°F (1.5°C).

Annual rainfall in the city averages 58 to 65 inches (1,490 mm), distributed relatively evenly.  March is the wettest month, averaging 6.93 inches (176 mm).  Thunderstorms, frequent throughout the year but especially common in summer, are a major source of precipitation.  Severe thunderstorms, sometimes producing damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes, occur occasionally, peaking in spring and again in autumn.

The region's economy was heavily reliant on its railroads in the early years.  Boasting five major rail lines and 44 daily trains, the city was Mississippi's largest at the dawn of the 20th century.  Its prosperity stemmed not only from the rail network itself, but also from the timber and cotton transported via these lines. This rail-dependent economy fueled significant regional and state-wide economic dominance from roughly 1890 to 1930.  While the 1950s saw a slowdown due to the railroad industry's decline, the city diversified, transitioning from a primarily rail-based economy to one driven by healthcare, military, and manufacturing sectors.

Meridian, Lauderdale County, and Marion share the East Mississippi Business Development Corporation, established in 1996 by local business leaders.  Despite a relatively small city civilian labor force of 15,420 (April 2010), Meridian's influence extends to a population of 232,900 within a 45-mile radius (72 km) and 526,500 within 65 miles (105 km), with corresponding labor forces of 104,600 and 234,200 respectively. This makes Meridian a regional center for jobs, retail, healthcare, and cultural activities.  Significantly, 80% of Lauderdale County's workforce lives in the county, with 90% residing within a 45-mile radius.

Lauderdale County's healthcare sector employed 6,260 individuals in April 2010.  Dominating the region, Rush Hospital had 2,610 employees, exceeding East Mississippi State Hospital (1,500) and Anderson Hospital (1,475). Meridian houses three hospitals and numerous other healthcare providers.  Jeff Anderson Regional Medical Center offers cardiovascular surgery, a Level II neonatal intensive care unit, and a fitness center.  Rush Foundation Hospital, part of Rush Health Systems, operates the Specialty Hospital of Meridian, providing extended care for patients needing prolonged hospital recovery.  Riley Hospital features two stroke treatment and rehabilitation centers.  Additional Meridian facilities include the Alliance Health Center and the historic East Mississippi State Hospital, established in 1882.

In April 2010, the retail sector was a significant source of employment in the county, providing jobs for 5,280 individuals.  Annual retail sales in the city approached $2 billion.  This robust sector is anchored by Bonita Lakes Mall, a 633,685-square-foot (58,871 m²) center featuring over 100 stores, restaurants, and a movie theater.  Further growth occurred with the November 2007 completion of Phase I of Meridian Crossroads, a 375,000-square-foot (34,800 m²) shopping center in the same area.  The North Hills Street shopping district also saw expansion, including new retail and office space near the Highway 19 Walmart Supercenter in March 2007.

Meridian boasts two significant military installations: Naval Air Station Meridian (NAS Meridian) and Key Field, contributing over 4,000 jobs to the local economy.  NAS Meridian trains naval aviators and other personnel, and notably hosts the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy, providing narcotics training for law enforcement across the Southeast.  Furthermore, Meridian houses the state's first Department of Homeland Security, leading a nine-county regional response team and a larger, twenty-nine-county task force. Key Field, site of the 1935 world endurance flight record set by the Key brothers, now houses the 186th Air Refueling Wing of the Air National Guard and supports the 185th Aviation Brigade of the Army National Guard.  An aviation history exhibit and the Meridian Aviation Museum are also located there.

Lauderdale County boasted 2,850 manufacturing jobs in April 2010.  Peavey Electronics, a prominent guitar, amplifier, and sound equipment manufacturer since 1965, is headquartered there.  Additional employers include Avery Dennison, Structural Steel Services, Sara Lee, Tower Automotive, and an unnamed corporation.  Four industrial parks further support the county's manufacturing sector.

Meridian's downtown area thrives economically thanks to the MSU Riley Center, which generates revenue through tourism, arts, and entertainment.  This venue draws over 60,000 visitors yearly for conferences, events, and performances.  Meanwhile, Loeb's Department Store, a Mississippi institution on Front Street, continues its legacy of four generations of family ownership. Since its 1887 founding by Alex Loeb, it has been a purveyor of high-quality men's and women's apparel.

Meridian boasts a rich artistic heritage spanning over a century, evidenced by its numerous arts organizations and vibrant cultural scene.  Founded in February 1933, the Meridian Art League (later the Meridian Art Association) was a pioneering arts group.  Initially showcasing exhibitions at the Lamar Hotel, the Association eventually secured a permanent home.  Following the closure of the Carnegie library, the Association renovated the building at 25th Ave and 7th St, opening the Meridian Museum of Art in 1970.  This museum now presents over thirty diverse annual exhibitions, encompassing traditional and contemporary art forms, including decorative arts, ethnographic pieces, photography, and sculpture,  with holdings ranging from 18th- and 19th-century portraits to 20th-century photography, and alongside a robust educational program.

Established in 1978, the Meridian Council for the Arts (MCA) serves as the official arts agency for Meridian and Lauderdale County.  Its annual activities include the Community Art Grants program, the annual [Name of Festival], various workshops, and other special events.  The MCA collaborates with numerous local arts organizations, such as the Meridian Museum of Art, the Meridian Little Theatre, and the Meridian Symphony Orchestra.  The Meridian Little Theatre, one of the South's oldest subscription-based community theaters (built in 1932), attracts over 22,000 attendees annually, making it Mississippi's most popular community theater.  Founded in 1961, the Meridian Symphony Orchestra (MSO) gave its inaugural concert in 1962, followed by its first full season in 1963.  In 1965, the MSO featured its first international soloist, Elena [Last Name].  The MSO also fostered the Meridian Public School District's orchestra and strings programs, and established the Meridian Symphony Chorus.  Currently led by Dr. Claire Fox Hillard (since 1991), the MSO will commemorate its 50th anniversary in February 2011 with a performance by Itzhak Perlman.

The Grand Opera House, constructed in 1889 by the half-brothers Israel Marks and Levi Rothenberg, showcased renowned performers and productions throughout its history, beginning with a German troupe's performance of Johann Strauss II's "The Gypsy Baron."  Following its closure in the late 1920s due to the Great Depression, the opera house remained vacant for almost seven decades.  A $10 million grant from the Riley Foundation (established in 1998) in 2000, supplemented by $15 million in combined city, county, and federal funding, initiated its restoration.  Reopened in September 2006 as the Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and Performing Arts, the renovated facility boasts a 950-seat auditorium, a 200-seat studio theater, and 30,000 square feet (2,787 m²) of meeting space, drawing over 60,000 annual visitors to downtown Meridian for events.

Meridian's remarkably preserved architecture from the early 20th century makes it a significant architectural destination.  Its wealth of buildings designed by renowned architects attracts architecture students from across the US and Canada.  Highland Park boasts the only surviving Southern US home by Canadian architect Louis S. Curtiss, inventor of the glass curtain wall skyscraper.  The Frank Fort-designed  <unk> Building, a prime example of Art Deco skyscrapers, rivals Detroit's Fisher Building.  California architect Wallace Neff, with family ties to Meridian and Selma's railroad industry, designed several Meridian homes, many on lower Poplar Springs Drive, comparable to Rudolph Valentino's Falcon Lair.  Sadly, one Neff design was lost to hospital expansion in 1990, and another burned in the 1950s.  The Meridian Post Office, an exceptional example of 1920s civic architecture, features bronze and Verde marble interiors.  Its original <unk> lighting, removed in the 1960s, is now found in private homes.

Meridian is slated to host the Mississippi Arts and Entertainment Center (MAEC).  The state legislature endorsed the project in 2001, pledging $4 million in 2006 contingent upon private fundraising of $8 million.  The city contributed $50,000 in September 2007.  The planned 175-acre (71 ha) MAEC at Bonita Lakes will feature an outdoor amphitheater, indoor concert hall, and a Hall of Fame celebrating Mississippi artists.  The Hall of Fame will occupy the renovated Montana's building downtown, purchased with the adjacent Meridian Hotel in July 2010 for $300,000.  To build anticipation, a Walk of Fame was unveiled outside the Riley Center in February 2009, beginning with Jimmie Rodgers.  B.B. King followed in September, and Tennessee Williams, Eudora Welty, William Faulkner, and Sela Ward were added by June 2010.  Future inductees into the Walk of Fame include Morgan Freeman, Jimmy Buffett, Elvis Presley, and Conway Twitty.

The city also boasts the <unk> Shrine Temple Theater, a significant venue for large-scale productions.  Its centerpiece is a 778-pipe Robert Morgan organ, one of only two original theater organs remaining in the state.  Originally seating 1800, the Temple thrived during the silent film era, then one of the largest stages in the US, second only to New York City's Roxy Theater. Now with a capacity of 1576, it hosts diverse year-round events including live performances, plays, concerts, <unk> Shrine activities, and classic film screenings.

Highland Park's Jimmie Rodgers Museum showcases the legendary "Singing Brakeman's" original guitar and other personal effects, alongside steam-era railroad artifacts.  Beyond the museum building, outdoor exhibits and a vintage locomotive are on display.  Meridian, Rodgers' birthplace, is commemorated with a Mississippi Blues Trail marker, highlighting his pioneering role in Mississippi blues, a distinction unique to a location outside the Delta.  Further honoring him, a Mississippi Country Music Trail marker was dedicated at Oak Grove Cemetery on June 1, 2010.  Since 1953, Meridian has annually celebrated Rodgers with a May festival marking his death anniversary.

Highland Park boasts a National Historic Landmark: a Dentzel carousel, crafted circa 1895 in Philadelphia.  Operating since 1909, this unique carousel—the world's only two-row stationary Dentzel menagerie—resides in its original building, constructed from Dentzel's blueprints.  Complementing this is "Around Town," a public art project featuring 62 carousel horse sculptures, sponsored by local businesses and individuals, and designed and painted by local artists. These sculptures are displayed throughout the city and county.

The city boasts several recreational parks: Highland Park, Bonita Lakes, and an unnamed lake.  Highland Park offers year-round access to picnic shelters, swimming pools, tennis courts, a baseball field, softball fields, and a playground. Bonita Lakes, a 3,300-acre (13 km²) city-owned park with three lakes, also features the Long Creek Reservoir, Lakeview Municipal Golf Course, nature trails, a fitness track, biking and horseback riding paths, pavilions, picnic areas, boat ramps, paddle boats, concessions, and fishing.  This area also includes Bonita Lakes Mall, Bonita Lakes Crossing, and Bonita Lakes Plaza. The unnamed lake, a 7,150-acre (28.9 km²) site with a 4,144-acre (16.77 km²) lake, provides boating, fishing, swimming, water skiing, picnicking, hunting, hiking, and camping.  Amenities include Splashdown Country Water Park, a 25-room motel, and cabins.

Meridian has hosted the annual State Games of Mississippi, a statewide multi-sport competition mirroring the Olympics, since 1992.  Affiliated with the National Congress of State Games and the U.S. Olympic Committee, the event has grown from 1,200 athletes in twelve sports in its inaugural year to over 70,000 participants.  The 2009 Games featured over 4,500 athletes across 27 sports.  State Games competitors are eligible for the Southeast Sports Festival, with medalists advancing to the biennial State Games of America.

The Meridian games, initially a single June weekend event, now span two weekends due to the addition of more sports.  Opening ceremonies commence on the third Friday of June in downtown Meridian.  Venues include Northeast Park (an 85-acre park on Highway 39 with extensive facilities), the  [Name of Complex] Davidson Complex, and other city fields.  Northeast Park boasts ten tennis courts, four softball fields, three soccer fields, a track, and a large pavilion. The [Name of Complex] Davidson Complex offers six tennis courts, four softball fields, and a half-mile track.  Additional locations include the Meridian Jaycee Soccer Complex, Sykes Park, and Phil Hardin Park.

The city boasts numerous golf courses, such as the public Lakeview Municipal Golf Course, an 18-hole course open daily.  Highway 39 North is home to the private Briarwood County Club, offering golf, swimming, fishing, and dining.  Additional golfing options in the city include Northwood Country Club, <unk> Creek Golf Center, and Ponta Creek Golf Course.

Amtrak's Crescent route links Meridian to New York City, Philadelphia, Baltimore, Washington, D.C., Charlotte, Atlanta, Birmingham, and New Orleans.  The Meridian Union Station Multi-Modal Transportation Center (1901 Front Street), situated within the National Register-listed Meridian Downtown Historic District, serves as a hub.  Originally constructed in 1906, rebuilt in 1997 after demolition in 1966, the station integrates various transportation options: Amtrak, the Meridian Transit System, Norfolk Southern Railway, Greyhound, Trailways, and other transit services.  Annual ridership across Amtrak trains, Greyhound buses, and Meridian Transit System buses averages 242,360 passengers.

Meridian Regional Airport, situated at Key Field on Airport Boulevard South, serves the city.  Located 3 miles (4.8 km) southwest of Meridian, its 10,004-foot (3,049 m) runway is Mississippi's longest public runway.  In operation since 1930, the airport provides daily flights to Dallas/Fort Worth, Texas.

Facing closure due to high maintenance costs during the Great Depression, the city's airport was saved in 1935 by a daring feat.  Airport managers Fred and Al Key flew their plane, the "Ole Miss," continuously for 27 days (June 4-July 1), achieving a record 653 hours and 34 minutes of flight. This publicity stunt generated sufficient funds and attention to secure the airport's future, leading to its renaming as Key Field in their honor.  Their record for sustained conventional flight remains unsurpassed.

Meridian's initial public school system, established under the 1870 Mississippi Constitution, operated from 1870 to 1885 under a Board of School Directors appointed by the City Council.  Prior to 1884,  approximately 400 students attended several privately-owned schools.  The city's first publicly-owned school opened in September 1884, while the first public school for African Americans utilized rented space at St. Paul Methodist Church.  A January 1888 state legislative amendment enabled Meridian to form its own municipal school district, followed by a March 1888 bond issue of $30,000 for new school construction.  This funding led to the 1894 construction of Wechsler School, the state's first brick public school building for Black students.

Meridian's Public School District, formed from an initial district and subsequent expansions, now comprises six elementary, three middle, and three high schools.  The city also boasts several private schools, such as Lamar, Calvary Christian, Community Christian, and St. Patrick's Catholic schools.  Meridian High School, the district's main high school, covers 37 acres (15 hectares), encompassing six buildings and 111 classrooms.  Serving grades 10-12, it has an enrollment of roughly 1,500 students.

Meridian boasts two post-secondary schools.  Meridian Community College (MCC), established in 1937, now resides at 910 Highway 19 N and provides free tuition for four semesters to local graduates (Meridian Public and Lauderdale County school districts, and homeschooled Lauderdale County residents).  Initially Meridian Junior College, housed at Meridian High School, it relocated in 1965. Following desegregation, it integrated with T.J. Harris Junior College in 1970, expanding its student body to include previously underserved African-American students.  The name changed to Meridian Community College in 1987 to better reflect its broadened scope.  A Mississippi State University campus also serves the city.  By Fall 2008, MCC enrolled 763 students from 33 Mississippi counties and several Alabama counties.

Meridian's public library, situated at 7th Street and 26th Avenue,  has a rich history.  Its origins trace back to the Fortnightly Book and Magazine Club, founded in the 1880s, which spearheaded fundraising efforts.  Their book collection formed the core of the city's first library.  Securing funding from Andrew Carnegie, thanks to local leader Israel Marks, resulted in two separate Carnegie libraries in 1913 – one for Black residents and one for white residents. The Black library, at 13th Street and 28th Avenue (on land donated by St. Paul Methodist Church), was unique, serving as Mississippi's sole Black library until after World War I and the only Carnegie library ever built for African Americans.  These segregated facilities operated until 1967, when the Civil Rights Act of 1964 prompted integration, merging their collections into the current library.  The former white library was repurposed as the Meridian Museum of Art (1970), while the former Black library was unfortunately demolished in 2008.

Established in 1898 as The Evening Star,  The Meridian Star is the city's sole daily newspaper.  Renamed in 1915, it's held that distinction since 1921.  Boasting a daily circulation of approximately 12,000 in March 2010,  it covers Lauderdale County and parts of western Alabama and eastern Mississippi.

While the Meridian Star is the city's sole remaining newspaper,  it's not the only one in its history.  The Memo Digest, for example, a 10-20 page publication of the 1970s, focused on African-American community issues and achieved a circulation of approximately 5,000.  Other past publications include The Colored Messenger, The State, The Weekly Mercury, The Blade, Weekly Echo, Fair Play, <unk>, Meridian Morning Sun, Teacher and Preacher, and Clarion.

Meridian, Mississippi's primary Designated Market Area (DMA) encompasses 72,180 television households.  WTOK-TV, an ABC affiliate based at 815 23rd Avenue, broadcasts from the city.  It operates two digital subchannels: a MyNetworkTV affiliate (WTOK-DT2) and Meridian's CW affiliate (WTOK-CD).  WMDN-TV, the NBC affiliate located at 1151 Crestview Circle, became the market's FOX affiliate on January 5, 2009, also airing some Retro Television Network (RTN) programming.  WMDN operates under a program services agreement with WDAM-TV, the CBS affiliate, which provides local news on its second subchannel.  Mississippi Public Broadcasting's local affiliate is WMPB-TV.

Meridian serves as the core city of the Meridian Arbitron Radio Market, encompassing a population of 64,500 individuals aged 12 and older.  In Fall 2009, FM 105.7, located on Highway 45 North, commanded the highest market share at 14.8%.  FM 104.1 followed with an 11.1% share, and AM 1010 held third place at 7.4%.  Additional popular stations included FM 97.9, FM 97.1, FM 106.9, AM 1450, and FM 95.1.  Mississippi Public Broadcasting is broadcast on FM 88.1.

Meridian, Mississippi native and Island Def Jam artist Big K.R.I.T. is renowned for his extensive catalog of mixtapes and albums, including *K.R.I.T. Wuz Here* and *4eva Na Day*.  His impressive fanbase is a testament to his lyrical prowess, self-produced beats, and stylistic versatility, seamlessly transitioning between introspective tracks like "The Vent" and energetic anthems such as "Mt. Olympus."

Situated west of mainland Shetland, Papa Stour is the eighth-largest of the Shetland Islands, encompassing 828 hectares (3.2 square miles).  Boasting a population under twenty, some of whom arrived following a 1970s resettlement initiative, the island is renowned for its dramatic coastal features.  Sea erosion of its volcanic rock has sculpted a remarkable landscape of caves, stacks, arches, blowholes, and cliffs.  This unique environment, along with its surrounding waters, supports a rich variety of wildlife.  The island's west side holds Site of Special Scientific Interest status, while the adjacent seas are designated a Special Area of Conservation.

The island boasts numerous Neolithic burial sites and the remnants of a 13th-century structure attributed to Duke Hakon, a relic of Norse settlement.  Its population peaked at 380 or more in the 19th century following the establishment of a fishing station at West Voe's <unk> location.  Population subsequently decreased, though it has rebounded from a 1970s low of 16.

Papa Stour, situated at St Magnus Bay's southwestern edge, boasts 34 kilometers (21 miles) of rugged, intricately indented coastline.  This coastline features numerous small inlets and four larger voes (Old Norse for "bay").  The southernmost voe offers the most sheltered anchorage, its cliffs framing a natural rock arch.  Eastward lies another voe (Old Norse: "house bay"), less secluded but serving as the island's primary harbor and ferry terminal.

Holm and Maiden Stack, guarding the southern harbor entrance, hold intriguing histories. Holm, a tidal island, served as a leper colony until the 1700s, though some believe vitamin deficiency, not leprosy, afflicted its inhabitants. Maiden Stack's name stems from a 14th-century tale of Lord Thorvald's small house, ruins still visible, built to protect his daughter.  However, she left pregnant, or, in another version, successfully eloped with a fisherman.  Northward, West Voe, its inner section known as [missing name], is the primary inlet;  Little Voe lies just west.

Dominating the island is the main settlement of <unk>, situated overlooking <unk> Voe.  East of the hill dyke (extending south from West Voe), it's encircled by low-lying land.  A 1.5 kilometer glacial moraine cuts across the western half of the island.  The remaining land largely comprises thin, stony soil, likely glacial till.  The island's near absence of peat, coupled with volcanic bedrock, results in relatively fertile soils. This peat scarcity historically led to "turf scalping" for fuel, leaving exposed rock in the interior.

Papa Stour Island, dating back to the Devonian period, consists of diverse volcanic and sedimentary rock formations.  During this time, Scotland resided on the Old Red Sandstone Continent, situated 10-25 degrees south of the equator.  Old Red Sandstone deposits (408-370 million years old) resulted from the erosion of uplifted Silurian rocks during the Pangaea formation, their subsequent deposition in river deltas.  A large freshwater lake, Lake Orcadie, bordered the eroding mountains, extending from Shetland to the southern Moray Firth.  The island's structure primarily comprises volcanic ash and lava, including rhyolite bands, from this era, though a Devonian fish bed also exists at Lamba Banks.  Numerous large boulders, remnants of Pleistocene glaciation, are also present.

Coastal erosion of the soft volcanic rock has sculpted a remarkable array of caves, stacks, arches, blowholes, cliffs, voes, and other formations, considered among Britain's finest.  The "Holl o' [Name of feature]" is a cave traversing the island's northwestern tip, nearly half a mile long and navigable by rowboat.  Similarly impressive is Christie's Hole in the southwest, part of whose roof collapsed in 1981.  Further west, near [Name of Voe], lies Francie's Hole, a favorite of Victorian memoirist John Tudor, who described it in his writings.

Papa Stour's waters teem with otters, grey seals, killer whales, and harbor porpoises.  The island also supports breeding colonies of Atlantic puffins, Arctic and common terns,  [unknown bird species], Arctic skuas, northern fulmars, common guillemots, razorbills, curlews, wheatears, ringed plovers, and great black-backed gulls.  Many migratory birds have also been sighted there.

Papa Stour boasts abundant wildflowers, such as mountain everlasting, spring squill, and  <unk>, alongside the common heather.  Its western shore holds Site of Special Scientific Interest status, while the surrounding waters are designated a Special Area of Conservation.  Shetland pony breeding continues as a traditional practice.

The island was settled around 3000 BC, evidenced by Neolithic burial chambers, known as "heel-shaped cairns."  Pre-Celtic and Celtic history remains obscure, but Norse arrival likely encountered a religious community.  The island's name, derived from  "<unk> <unk>", translates to "Big Island of the Papar" (Celtic monks), differentiating it from the smaller Papa Little, 12 kilometers (7.5 miles) to the west.

A 1299 Old Norse manuscript, Shetland's oldest extant record, details a dramatic event at the home of Duke Hakon Magnusson (later King Hakon V of Norway).  Near  <unk> Voe, stone circle remnants mark a "ting," or local assembly, site of a duel.  Lord Thorvald <unk>, accused of corruption in the manuscript and later styled "dominus de <unk>", won this duel. (His daughter's tragic tale is mentioned elsewhere.)  Ruins of Duke Hakon's 13th-century dwelling remain near <unk> Voe.

Shetland nominally fell under Scottish rule in 1469, but Norse landowners retained their Papa Stour holdings until the 17th century.  Bremen and Hamburg merchants established a seasonal trading post in the 16th century to purchase fish from Shetland's fishing fleet.  By the 18th century, two Scottish lairds, Thomas Gifford of Busta and Arthur Nicolson of Lerwick, owned the island and oversaw a thriving deep-sea (Old Norse: 'djúpsjá') fishing industry, utilizing six-oared boats, known as [missing boat name], during the summer.

Built in 1806, the island church overlooks Kirk Sand in Fore Wick Bay.  Approximately 300 meters away, possibly on the headland between Kirk Sand's west end and [Bay Name], lies a suspected older chapel site dating back to the 12th century (or earlier). Locally known as "[Chapel Name] kirk," the Ordnance Survey designates it as the remains of a medieval chapel.  Legend claims supernatural forces hampered construction, undoing each day's work.  These forces, it's said, relocated the foundation stones to the current church site, enabling its completion.  A 2004 excavation yielded few artifacts—mostly large rhyolite blocks and whalebone— lending some credence to the local folklore.

West Voe's fishing station, established in the 19th century, supported a population exceeding 360 on Papa Stour.  However,  fuel scarcity and the steam drifter's impact on fishing led to population decline from the 1870s onward.  This period also saw a notable event: Edwin Lindsay, an Indian army officer and son of the 6th Earl of Balcarres, was exiled to the island after a court-martial for refusing to fight.  He endured 26 years of confinement before Quaker Catherine Watson secured his release in 1835.  Lindsay's Well, a spring in the island's south, marks the site of his permitted bathing.

Near Dutch Loch, several well-preserved horizontal watermills, also called Norse or Clack Mills, stand as testament to a bygone era.  These were typically two-story structures with turf roofs, built into embankments for convenient access to the upper floor housing the millstone.  A stationary lower millstone was paired with a rotating upper one, powered by water impacting paddles beneath.  Some remained operational on Papa Stour into the early 1900s, and a functional example survives on the Burn of [unk], at [unk] in Shetland's southern Mainland.

Like many small Scottish islands, Papa Stour's population reached its zenith in the 19th century, subsequently experiencing a sharp decrease (similar to Mingulay).  The island school closed by 1970, leaving just sixteen elderly inhabitants.  An advert in Exchange and Mart, offering a croft and five sheep free, however, attracted numerous applicants, boosting the population to 33 by 1981.  Internal disputes culminating in legal battles caused a population drop to 20 by 2005, forcing the school's closure again.  A family's departure in early 2008 reduced the number to nine.  The 2011 census reported 15 residents, contrasting with a 4% overall increase (to 103,702) in Scottish island populations during that decade.

On March 28th, 1930, the Aberdeen fishing vessel Ben Doran sank on the Ve Skerries, three miles northwest of Papa Stour, while en route to Scalloway to unload its catch.  Despite relatively calm seas at the time of grounding, the wreck wasn't discovered until the next day by a passing trawler.  Subsequent rescue efforts by the coastguard and local volunteers were hampered by worsening weather, rendering access to the skerries impossible.  Although a call for assistance was sent to the Stromness lifeboat in Orkney (120 miles distant), it arrived too late.  Tragically, all nine crew members died; only three bodies—those of James Mitchell (returned to Aberdeen) and J. Cormack and J.R. [unknown] (buried in Scalloway)—were recovered.

In February 1940, the SS Highcliffe, a cargo vessel, struck <unk> Holm in foggy conditions.  Fortunately, the weather was otherwise mild, resulting in the loss of only the ship and its cargo.  Later, in 1967, the Aberdeen trawler Juniper grounded in Lyra Sound, near 60-meter (200-foot) cliffs.  All twelve crew members were saved by the <unk> lifeboat; the coxswain received the RNLI silver medal for this daring rescue.

On December 9th, 1977, the Aberdeen trawler Elinor Viking, captained by Alec Flett, sank on Papa Stour's Ve Skerries.  High seas prevented the local lifeboat from reaching the crew.  Responding to Coastguard Station Officer Alec Webster's call, a British Airways Sikorsky helicopter from Sumburgh Airport rescued all crew members via winch, despite gale-force winds.  The helicopter crew received accolades for their courageous rescue.  Although no lives were lost, this event led to a 1979 lighthouse construction on the skerries and possibly influenced the establishment of Sumburgh Airport's current Search and Rescue helicopter unit.

Island life centers on crofting, with sheep underpinning agriculture, though diverse livestock—cattle, pigs, goats, poultry—are also raised.  Vegetables are cultivated, frequently within protective circular walls, known as 'scrubs'.  Fishing persists, albeit on a limited scale.  A pier houses the post office, but lacks a shop.  Main electricity arrived only at the century's end.  The Papa Stour Project, a Christian-supported facility, provides housing for men battling drug and alcohol addiction. Ferries now connect Papa Stour to the Shetland Mainland across the Sound of Papa, a 45-minute journey. While the ferry accommodates cars, the island boasts only one short road.  The four main voes offer safe anchorage for visiting yachts, yet strong tidal currents in the Sound of Papa and northwest demand caution.

It's also the inspiration for the poem "Da Sang o da Papa men," now a folk song thanks to <unk> Manson's musical arrangement.  The memorable and repetitive chorus, " <unk> Foula Doon!", is especially powerful.

The phrase "<unk> Foula <unk>!" depicts the Shetland fishing practice of rowing far out to sea, beyond sight of Foula's cliffs—approximately 96 kilometers west of Papa Stour.  This journey exposed them to "tide-lumps," exceptionally large waves caused by wind opposing tide. The poem's powerful conclusion evokes the fishermen's return, guided by the scent of home across the water. This vividly portrays the sensory experience, a hallmark of <unk>'s style.  The poem's resonance is deepened by the fact that Da Horn o Papa, a significant geographical landmark, collapsed around the time of its writing, making it a lament not only for a lost lifestyle but also a lost landmark.

Slayer's 1986 album *Reign in Blood* begins with "Angel of Death," a song written by guitarist Jeff Hanneman.  Inspired by the horrific human experimentation of Nazi doctor Josef Mengele at Auschwitz, the track's lyrics and music have drawn persistent accusations of Nazi sympathy and racism against the band throughout their history.

Although "Angel of Death" sparked debate and contributed to *Reign in Blood*'s delayed release, it remains a staple of Slayer's live performances, appearing on all their live albums and DVDs, and even making its way into several films.  Critics lauded the song; AllMusic's Steve Huey, for instance, called it a "classic."

During a Slayer tour, guitarist Jeff Hanneman encountered books about Josef Mengele, the Nazi doctor.  This sparked the inspiration for "Angel of Death." Hanneman recalled purchasing two books about Mengele, describing the content as "sick shit," which heavily influenced the song's lyrics when the band began recording.

"Angel of Death" describes Josef Mengele's horrific World War II medical experiments at Auschwitz.  Targeting groups like twins and dwarfs, his research encompassed physical and psychological torture.  The song cites examples including unanesthetized surgeries, blood transfusions between twins, lethal gas exposure, injections of deadly pathogens, organ and limb removal, sex reassignment attempts, and prolonged isolation, all inflicted on his victims.

The penultimate verse's line, "joined heads...rip yourselves apart," alludes to accusations against Josef Mengele.  Survivor Vera Alexander testified at Adolf Eichmann's 1961 trial, claiming Mengele sewed together twins, one deformed, back-to-back, wrists intertwined, allegedly "sewing their veins together" to create "Siamese twins."  This allegation gained wider recognition through the 1985 documentary *The Search for Mengele*, referenced by authors like Mengele expert Gerald Posner.

Slayer's 1986 album, *Reign in Blood*, faced a release delay because of the controversial lyrics in "Angel of Death."  Def Jam, the band's label, initially partnered with Columbia Records for distribution, but Columbia rejected the album citing concerns over both the lyrical content and the album art, which they considered excessively violent.  Consequently, Geffen Records ultimately released *Reign in Blood* on October 7, 1986, but the album's contentious nature prevented its inclusion in Geffen's official release schedule.
